name: Beth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I look after the laying hens at Pryce's, out past the end of Mill Street. Twelve thousand free-range birds in three sheds. I'm in at half six, walk every shed, check water lines, feeders, any dead birds, then I open the pop holes so they can get out on the range. The eggs come in on belts to the packing room and I grade and stack trays till lunch. What I love is the walk in the morning, when you can hear if a shed's happy. What wears me out is the dust and the record book, because Mr Pryce wants everything typed into the new app and I still write it on paper first.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Because paper doesn't freeze when you've got gloves on. And because I trust my own handwriting more than a screen. Mr Pryce's son Owen set up the app and he means well, but I've never used any of that AI stuff and I don't plan to. My partner Dani's a care worker, she laughs at me, says I'm eighty years old inside. We rent a little terrace on Mill Street. We've got about three months of money put by, which is more than most people our age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So basically what we've got now, just a bit more of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everyone at the feed merchant's was going on about robots taking over, and here we are, still collecting eggs. I'd say the real problem in farming was never computers, it's the supermarkets paying us pennies for a dozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means Owen's app gets a bit smarter and nags me more. Maybe it spots a sick bird earlier, fine. But my job stays my job. The thing that actually threatens me is bird flu, not AI. In 2022 we had a case two farms over and I didn't sleep for a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep my head down, keep doing the morning walk, maybe finally let Owen show me the app properly so he stops sighing at me. I'd keep putting a bit by each month like we do now, and I'd keep pushing the farm workers' union stuff at the pub, because pay is still the fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest. It's the world I already know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union. Are you a member?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am, since last year. There's only four of us from round here. I joined after Mr Pryce cut our overtime rate and nobody said a word. In this picture that's still what I'd care about, a fair rate, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dani say if you told her AI turned out to be hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, because at her work they keep promising a computer that does the care notes and it never works. We'd probably have a laugh about it over tea. Then she'd tell me to learn the app anyway.

S0.say: I'd tell people I always said the robot talk was overblown. I'd say the real problem in farming is still supermarkets paying farmers pennies for a dozen eggs.
S0.think: Privately I think Owen's app gets a bit smarter and maybe spots sick birds sooner, but my job stays my job. Bird flu scares me far more than computers do.
S0.do: Carries on with the daily shed walks and keeps saving a little each month. Lets Owen show her the app properly and keeps pushing for fair pay through the farm workers' union.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, because it's the world she already knows.
S0.quote: The thing that actually threatens me is bird flu, not AI.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is happiest when nothing changes, and she reads this picture as proof she was right. Her energy goes to pay and supermarket prices, not technology. The paper record book is a small but telling sign of how she meets anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That one sounds more real to me than the first, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the farm workers need a seat at the table before the machines arrive, not after. At the union meeting I'd be the one saying, write it down now, nobody loses their job without retraining paid by the company. Online I'd share stuff about it, but I don't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the one who'd struggle. Owen would bring in a robot that walks the sheds and picks out floor eggs, and he'd want me to run it from a tablet. I'd be slow at that. I'm good with birds, not screens, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit to see what Mr Pryce actually buys. Then, if the robot comes, I'd ask for proper training in work time, not a video. I'd stop the takeaways on Fridays and put more in savings, maybe get us up to five months. And I'd get the other three union lads to back me on a written deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the weather forecast says maybe snow, and you lie awake listening for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what he buys. Why not get ahead of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust the sales talk. My uncle bought a fancy egg counter in 2019 and it broke in a month. I'd rather see it work in our shed first. That's not lazy, that's just careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who does the egg packing. He's fifty-something and his English isn't great, and packing is the first thing a machine takes. I'd worry about him before me.

S1.say: I'd say farm workers need a written deal before the machines arrive, with retraining paid by the company. I'd raise it at the union meeting and share a few posts online.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she'd be the one who struggles, because a shed robot run from a tablet plays to her weak spot. She's good with birds, not screens, and she knows it.
S1.do: Waits to see what equipment the farm actually buys, then asks for real training in work time. Drops Friday takeaways to build savings toward five months and rallies union colleagues for a written agreement.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like lying awake listening for snow that might come.
S1.quote: I'm good with birds, not screens, and I know it.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is collective and confident, but privately she's worried about her own slowness with technology. She waits for proof partly from caution and partly from fear of looking clumsy. Her first worry for others goes to an older packer, Marek, which says a lot about her values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's three flocks. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loud and clear that this was done to us by tech companies and nobody voted for it. I'd be at every protest going. I'd tell anyone who'd listen that the government has to pay people while they find something else, because it's not our fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? I'm finished in farming. If a robot can walk the sheds, grade eggs, and spot a sick hen better than me, Mr Pryce would be mad to keep paying me. And I've got no other trade. I left school for the poultry course and that's all I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd cut everything: no holiday, no new car, Dani's and my savings stay untouched. I'd sign every petition and go to the union march. When it arrived I'd apply for whatever support there was, and I'd ask Dani's manager if they're hiring in care, because people will still want a person to hold their hand, surely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A sort of cold feeling, like walking into a shed and finding it gone quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. With two years I can't learn a new trade properly, I can't save enough to matter. I'd be falling, not stepping. If it was longer I might at least choose where I land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would you start now, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds daft. But if it's going to take my job anyway, learning it just feels like helping it pack my bags. I'd rather spend those two years with the hens and the union.

S2.say: I'd say this was done to us by tech companies and nobody voted for it. I'd be at every protest and say the government must pay people while they find new work.
S2.think: Off the record she thinks she's finished in farming, because a robot that walks sheds and grades eggs makes her too expensive. She has no other trade to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts all extra spending at once and protects the couple's savings. Joins union marches and petitions, then applies for any public support and asks about care jobs where her partner works.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a cold feeling like walking into a shed that has gone quiet.
S2.quote: Learning it just feels like helping it pack my bags.
S2.fieldNote: With two years she sees no time to retrain and falls back on protest and public help. Her refusal to learn AI tools is emotional, not practical, and she knows it. Care work, her partner's field, is the only door she can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's still fast, but it's not tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message really, but calmer. I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, make the companies pay into a fund for workers like us. I'd want the union pushing that with the government from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the job. But five years is enough to train for something. I think I'd go into care, like Dani. It scares me less than computers do, and I'm good at noticing when something's off, with hens or with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd ask Dani's work about the care certificate, part-time, maybe two evenings a week. I'd keep doing the hens till they don't need me. We'd push savings up to six months. And I'd write to our MP, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a bit of hope in it. It's the difference between being pushed and walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Care work could change too in this picture. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I have, and I don't know. Maybe robots lift people in and out of bed. But I can't believe people would want a machine holding their mum's hand at the end. If I'm wrong about that, I'm wrong about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mr Pryce when you started the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him straight, I'm not leaving you in the lurch, I'll stay till the robots are in. He's not a bad man. He's squeezed by the supermarkets same as me.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so let's use them and make the tech companies pay into a fund for workers. I'd want the union pushing the government on it from the start.
S3.think: Privately she still expects to lose the job, but five years is enough to train for care work. She trusts her knack for noticing when something's wrong, with hens or with people.
S3.do: Starts a part-time care certificate two evenings a week while staying on with the hens. Raises savings to six months and writes to her MP for the first time.
S3.feel: Anxious but with some hope, because she would be walking rather than being pushed.
S3.quote: It's the difference between being pushed and walking.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years turn her from protest-only into someone with a plan. She still avoids anything to do with computers and picks the most human job she can think of. She doesn't blame her boss; she sees him as squeezed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. Huh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance, and if we waste it that's on the government. I'd be at the union saying, plan it now, train people now, don't wait for year nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, part of me would think, ten years, that might not even happen, they always say these things. So I might drag my feet. But I'd know deep down the hens wouldn't need me by the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the hens for a good few years, it's what I love. Around year three or four I'd start the care training, slowly. We'd save, and maybe Dani and I would finally talk about kids, because I'd want them settled before it all lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not panicked. Ten years feels like a long winter you can stock up for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said part of you might drag your feet. What would stop you doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani. She'd keep on at me. And seeing it happen at other farms. If the place out on the bypass got robot sheds and laid people off, that'd shift me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does ten years compare with two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm falling. Ten years, I'm choosing. The worst bit about ten is I might waste it, because I'm slow to move. I'd want someone holding me to it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance, and wasting it would be the government's fault. At the union I'd push for planning and training now, not in year nine.
S4.think: Privately part of her would doubt it would happen and she might drag her feet. Deep down she'd still know the hens wouldn't need her by the end.
S4.do: Keeps working with the hens for several years, then starts care training around year three or four. Builds savings and begins planning children with her partner so the family is settled before the change lands.
S4.feel: Uneasy but not panicked, like facing a long winter she can stock up for.
S4.quote: Two years, I'm falling. Ten years, I'm choosing.
S4.fieldNote: Beth is honest that a long warning could make her slower, not faster. She needs a push from her partner or a visible layoff nearby to act. The decade turns her talk from defence to family plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years and I've got no other trade, no time to learn one, and three months of money. What would help is the government paying people a wage while they retrain, and the training being with people, in person, not on an app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. Everyone asks about jobs. But a robot doesn't hear when a shed's gone quiet. Maybe it will one day. I'd still want someone to ask whether that matters.

headlineQuote: Two years, I'm falling. Ten years, I'm choosing.
portrait: Beth Garcia is a 27-year-old who runs the laying sheds for 12,000 free-range hens on a family farm, and still writes her records on paper before typing them into the farm app. She lives with her partner Dani, a care worker, in a rented terrace and has about three months saved. She leans left, backs the union and blames supermarkets and tech firms rather than her boss. Slow with technology and proud of it, she sees AI Plateau as proof she was right, but in the AGI pictures she expects to lose farming altogether. With two years she falls back on protest and public help; with five or ten she plans a move into care work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she has no other trade, no time to learn one and only about three months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A wage paid by the government while people retrain, with training given in person rather than through an app.
